goals: Understand how optimization and regularization affect singular-value spectra and the effective rank of weight matrices.
Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.
Understand the geometry and practical language-model fine-tuning behavior of LoRA and other low-rank updates.
Evaluate tradeoffs among model quality, memory, throughput, and communication cost across model scales.
Build an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

Recent work on SVDQuant mitigates the errors introduced through FP4 quantization for diffusion models by adding high-precision low-rank corrections obtained via SVD. However, this high-precision low-rank correction requires many bits per rank, and it runs on the same tensor cores as the main FP4 GEMM. matches.title: LoRASpace: A Pool-Wide Shared Substrate for Static and Dynamic Multi-LoRA Composition
matches.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) attaches small low-rank matrices to a frozen backbone, and public repositories host many LoRAs per backbone, each for a different concept or task. matches.title: Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment for LLM Reasoning over Temporal Knowledge Graphs

passages.text: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

Scaling laws ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) motivate larger models for improved quality, while their memory and computational demands increase reliance on cloud infrastructure with high-end accelerators. However, network connectivity can be unstable in underwater and rescue operations ( Stojanovic & Preisig, 2009 ; Deng et al., 2013 ; Gunn & Anderson, 2015 ) . Safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving require on-device decisions to avoid cloud communication delays ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Kuutti et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Bodmer et al., 2026 ) , while privacy requirements can prevent sensitive data from being uploaded ( European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016 ; Shi et al., 2016 ) . These constraints require large-model inference to move from the cloud to resource-constrained edge devices. Fitting large models within limited memory and achieving low inference latency with the available computational resources are the two critical challenges of this transition. The latency requirement is particularly important in feedback control, where inference latency adds to loop delay and excessive delays can degrade closed-loop performance or destabilize the system, compromising safety ( Shin & Cui, 1995 ; Findeisen & Allgöwer, 2004 ; Ma et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Nan et al., 2026 ) .

To address memory constraints, existing compression methods use quantization ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , distillation ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , pruning ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , and low-rank factorization ( Hsu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . Varying memory budgets across edge devices call for elastic compression of a single trained checkpoint to multiple model sizes. SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) enables such elastic compression by learning sparse-and-low-rank (SLR) representations for each linear projection 1 1 1 Here, linear projection refers to a learned linear map in the attention (query/key/value/output) or multi-layer perceptron (MLP; up/gate/down) modules. Embeddings and the language model head are excluded unless noted. during pretraining. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into lower inference latency. Unstructured SLR saves static memory but incurs higher inference latency (see Appendix A.1 ). We identify the overhead from irregular memory access in unstructured sparse operations as a critical barrier to deploying large models on edge devices. Hardware-friendly patterns, including block sparsity ( Okanovic et al., 2025 ) , N : M N\!:\!M sparsity ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , and row-/column-wise sparsity ( Wen et al., 2016 ) , are therefore required to translate these memory savings into efficient edge inference. A straightforward extension of SALAAD is to impose these patterns on its learned sparse components after pretraining. However, our experiments show that this post-hoc conversion can sharply degrade model performance (see Appendix A.2 ). We therefore induce structured sparsity during pretraining , allowing the SLR components to adapt jointly to the structural constraints.

Compression methods for large language models broadly divide into pruning, low-rank factorization, and quantization. Unstructured pruning removes individual weights by magnitude ( Han et al., 2015 ) or calibration-based criteria ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ) , while low-rank methods such as SVD-LLM ( Wang et al., 2025c ) factorize weight matrices and SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) shrinks them by removing channels. A second post-hoc family instead runs iterative ADMM on the pretrained weights: ELSA ( Lee et al., 2026 ) pushes unstructured sparsity to extreme ratios, and 3BASiL ( Makni et al., 2025 ) performs layer-wise SLR reconstruction via a 3-block ADMM–both are data-hungry and take hours of GPU-time to compress a single model. Compression-aware pretraining instead induces compressibility during training: LORO ( Mo et al., 2025 ) pretrains in a preset low-rank subspace, SLTrain ( Han et al., 2024 ) augments low-rank pretraining with a fixed-support sparse component, and SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) jointly learns SLR components via ADMM. The sparse components in SLTrain and SALAAD are unstructured and do not map efficiently onto accelerator primitives. LOST ( Li et al., 2025 ) combines low-rank factors with channel-wise sparsity, but its preset rank and sparse capacity fix the model size during training, and its formulation does not support elastic deployment across budgets from a single checkpoint. It also inserts an additional nonlinearity between the low-rank factors, changing the underlying model architecture. S-SALAAD preserves the original architecture and supports multiple structured sparsity patterns, learning a representation that can be compressed from a single checkpoint to different parameter budgets.

passages.text: We test post-hoc block compression by applying energy-guided alternating refinement (EGAR; Section 4.2 ) to the same SALAAD Llama-1B checkpoint pretrained with unstructured sparsity, under different block constraints and parameter budgets. Table 2 reveals two trends. First, at a fixed budget, perplexity rises as the imposed blocks become coarser. Second, with coarser blocks, perplexity increases more steeply as the parameter budget decreases. These trends are consistent with the reduced pruning flexibility of coarser blocks. Grouping more weights into a single pruning unit restricts which weights can be retained at a given budget, limiting the compressed model’s representational capacity. A checkpoint pretrained with unstructured sparsity has not adapted to these constraints, making post-hoc pruning more damaging as the budget tightens. These results motivate inducing the target structure during pretraining, allowing the sparse and low-rank components to adapt to it under the task loss. To this end, we introduce S-SALAAD ( S tructured- S parse- A nd- L ow-Rank A daptation via AD MM), a plug-and-play framework that learns structured SLR representations during pretraining for elastic compression and efficient edge inference. Based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), it induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture or optimizer update rules. Efficient low-rank updates reduce pretraining overhead, while budget-aware refinement enables zero-shot compression of a single checkpoint to multiple parameter budgets without calibration data or further training. Among these patterns, we identify block sparsity as a practical choice for elastic deployment given current technical capabilities. With dedicated CPU and GPU kernels, the resulting models advance the perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier relative to the evaluated baselines. Our contributions are summarized as follows: ❖ A plug-and-play framework for structured-sparsity learning. S-SALAAD jointly learns model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components under the task loss, adapting the representation to structural constraints during pretraining. S-SALAAD induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture, and it is compatible with existing optimizers.

❖ A practical end-to-end implementation. To support the training of larger models and their edge deployment, we address bottlenecks in the training, compression, and inference stages. Specifically, we use i) a warm-started iterative singular value decomposition (I-SVD) to reduce the computational overhead of low-rank updates during pretraining ii) energy-guided alternating refinement (EGAR) to enable zero-shot compression without calibration data or further training, allocating the parameter budget across projections without a preset sparse–low-rank split and reducing reconstruction error within the allocated capacities iii) dedicated CPU and GPU kernels to exploit the induced structured sparsity and reduce inference latency . ❖ Empirical Pareto frontier across training settings. S-SALAAD advances the empirical perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier across hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines, with each checkpoint supporting multiple compression budgets. These gains hold for Llama2-1B pretraining and cross-architecture distillation from Nemotron-3-Super-120B to Qwen3-1.7B. ❖ Analysis of structured representations. S-SALAAD provides an explicit structured representation of Transformer weights, enabling us to identify distinct sparsity characteristics across linear projection types. Our analysis identifies block sparsity as a practical choice for advancing the perplexity-memory-latency Pareto frontier, combining flexible compression with efficient execution on CPUs and GPUs. Furthermore, we also reveal the relationship between tolerable block granularity and model scale, providing empirical guidance for selecting block sizes when extending S-SALAAD to larger models.

Comparison of sparsity patterns. Figure 5 compares perplexity against parameter count for block, : 4 2\!:\!4 , and row-/column-wise sparsity on Llama-350M. Although : 4 2\!:\!4 sparsity achieves lower perplexity at the largest budgets, its fixed sparse capacity restricts elastic compression, with perplexity rising sharply as the parameter count decreases. Block and row-/column-wise sparsity instead maintain competitive perplexity over a wider budget range. Figure 5: Perplexity vs. parameter count on Llama-350M. Heatmaps of the sparse components learned with S-SALAAD reveal pronounced row- or column-aligned patterns in attention projections (Appendices E.2 and E.3 ). This organization helps explain why the additional pruning freedom of blocks does not yield a clear advantage over row-/column-wise sparsity in the perplexity–parameter curves. With comparable quality trade-offs, the efficient mapping of block computations onto current hardware motivates our focus on block sparsity and the development of dedicated CPU and GPU kernels. This choice reflects current hardware and deployment requirements; other patterns may become preferable as these evolve, and S-SALAAD’s unified formulation accommodates such alternatives. Within each model scale, the variants share the same base training configuration, with their settings for structure induction detailed in Appendix D.3 . Finer blocks impose weaker structural constraints and allow more flexible allocation of sparse capacity during compression. This benefit is evident for the × 8 8\!\times\!8 and × 16 16\!\times\!16 variants on both Llama-350M and Llama-1B at tight budgets (Figures 6(a) and 6(b) ). For example, at 500M parameters on Llama-1B, their perplexities are 17.07 and 17.03, respectively, compared with 17.86 for L L -only.

To this end, we introduce S-SALAAD ( S tructured- S parse- A nd- L ow-Rank A daptation via AD MM), a plug-and-play framework that learns structured SLR representations during pretraining for elastic compression and efficient edge inference. Based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), it induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture or optimizer update rules. Efficient low-rank updates reduce pretraining overhead, while budget-aware refinement enables zero-shot compression of a single checkpoint to multiple parameter budgets without calibration data or further training. Among these patterns, we identify block sparsity as a practical choice for elastic deployment given current technical capabilities. With dedicated CPU and GPU kernels, the resulting models advance the perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier relative to the evaluated baselines. S-SALAAD induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture, and it is compatible with existing optimizers.

passages.text: Muon, a 2024-born optimizer for language models, differs from the 2015-born spectral gradient descent [ 1 , 2 ] mainly in its fast, GPU-friendly Newton–Schulz polynomial for orthogonalizing the gradient matrix. Accordingly, a line of research proposes faster polynomial iterations for gradient orthogonalization, such as Polar Express and Gram Newton--Schulz , both built on quintic polynomials. In this paper, we introduce Polar Switch , a new approach to polynomial gradient orthogonalization. Using simple polynomial circuits, Polar Switch reaches a given high polynomial degree at a lower FLOP cost than quintic iterations. We define a circuit as a short sequence of symmetric matrix products on a few square buffers, and circuits with k k products form a restricted family of odd polynomials of degree up to 2 k + 1 + 1 2^{k+1}+1 . We choose the sequence of products in each circuit, their coefficients, and how the circuits are composed by numerically minimizing a worst-case bound on the polar approximation error. This minimization is subject to a FLOP budget that accounts for symmetric matrix multiplication kernels and a rounding constraint for numerical stability in half precision. Our two recommended Polar Switch methods have 15.5–18.7% lower runtime than Polar Express on square matrices and 8.6–16.2% lower runtime than Gram Newton--Schulz on rectangular matrices with aspect ratios 3.25, 3.5, and 8, with comparable approximation accuracy. In pretraining Modded-NanoGPT #91, Qwen3-0.6B, and Gemma 3-1B, Polar Switch reaches final validation losses similar to those of established orthogonalization methods. Across the more than 14 million matrices that each of the two recommended methods orthogonalized in these runs, the estimated output spectral norms never exceed the designed

orthogonalization methods. Across the more than 14 million matrices that each of the two recommended methods orthogonalized in these runs, the estimated output spectral norms never exceed the designed bounds by more than 3%, demonstrating their numerical stability.

We make three contributions. (i) We introduce Polar Switch , a FLOP-efficient orthogonalization method for Muon based on high-degree polynomial circuits. (ii) We develop efficient GPU implementations of Polar Switch with two or three square buffers. Each kernel combines a matrix product and its additions before one float16 store, and we select coefficients that try to keep this half-precision computation numerically stable. (iii) Across three LLM pretraining setups, Polar Switch reaches final validation losses similar to those of established orthogonalization methods. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 presents Polar Switch , explains how we design its circuits and coefficients under a FLOP budget, and describes its GPU implementation. Section 4 compares Polar Switch with quintic baselines in LLM pretraining, runtime, and approximation accuracy. Appendix A gives the theory, the numerical search, and the coefficients of Polar Switch . Appendix B gives the detailed experimental setup for LLM pretraining and the runtime and approximation accuracy experiments.

Equivalent formulas can round differently because their intermediate computations differ [ 50 ] , and small singular values are sensitive to reduced precision [ 51 ] . Mixed precision is studied in linear algebra [ 52 , 53 , 54 ] and training [ 55 , 56 ] . Gram Newton--Schulz [ 16 ] accumulates square multipliers between rectangular updates, and Dion3 [ 57 ] uses it for distributed training. AMO [ 58 ] adapts iteration counts, Dion [ 59 ] uses low-rank updates, Dion2 [ 60 ] selects rows or columns, Hierarchical Muon [ 61 ] uses tiles, and CacheMuon [ 62 ] reuses transforms. Turbo-Muon [ 63 ] uses an almost-orthogonal preconditioner for faster updates, and PRISM [ 64 ] computes matrix functions adaptively. IFNSO [ 65 ] replaces the iterations with one polynomial in selected matrix powers and learns its coefficients. A cubic Newton–Schulz schedule [ 66 ] uses ten instead of fifteen dominant matrix products and reaches a similar validation loss. MuonBP [ 67 ] , CMuon [ 68 ] , and DMuon [ 69 ] support distributed computation. Polar Switch builds on polynomial Newton–Schulz iterations with efficient GPU implementations.

We introduced Polar Switch , which replaces the quintic iterations in Muon with a few polynomial circuits of high degree. We select these circuits and their coefficients under a FLOP budget, and our GPU implementations run them in float16 on two or three square buffers. In our experiments, PS2-55 and PS3-55 reduced runtime by 15.5–18.7% relative to Polar Express on square matrices and by 8.6–16.2% relative to Gram Newton--Schulz on rectangular matrices, and they gave final validation losses similar to those of established orthogonalization methods in LLM pretraining.

matches.abstract_excerpt: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. matches.title: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization
matches.abstract_excerpt: Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. matches.title: PFedQFT: Personalized Federated Quantum-Inspired Fine-Tuning for Medical Large Language Models
matches.abstract_excerpt: Medical data remain fragmented across institutional silos because of privacy, governance, and ownership constraints. Federated learning enables medical institutions to adapt large language models (LLMs) collaboratively without transferring raw records. However, independently parameterized low-rank adapters incur repeated parameter and communication costs across Transformer projections, while uniform aggregation may limit adaptation to heterogeneous institutional data. We propose PFedQFT, a quantum-inspired framework for personalized federated fine-tuning with a compact shared adapter. Specifically, PFedQFT constructs reusable orthonormal adaptation bases from compact skew-symmetric generators using a truncated matrix-exponential approximation followed by QR orthonormalization. matches.title: E8-QAT: Efficient 2-Bit Quantization-Aware Training with Implicit Lattice Codebooks
matches.abstract_excerpt: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint of large language models, but preserving accuracy with efficient training remains challenging. Scalar quantization encodes weights independently, while explicit-codebook vector quantization introduces costly search during training. We propose E8-QAT, a 2-bit quantization-aware training framework that uses the $E_8$ lattice as an implicit eight-dimensional codebook. It jointly quantizes weight groups through arithmetic projection without storing or searching an explicit codebook during the training forward pass. A 2-bit core encoding and sparse extension preserve the selected lattice points exactly, adding less than 0.1\% to core index storage. matches.title: On the gradient conjecture at infinity: Finite spherical length for gradient trajectories of definable potentials
matches.abstract_excerpt: We prove that for every open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ the spherical projection of every gradient trajectory $θ(t)$, $t \geq 0$, of a definable $C^1$-potential $F \colon U \to \mathbb{R}$ has finite length and, in particular, converges (directional convergence). matches.abstract_excerpt: We study a reactive optimizer that uses a pretrained language-model agent to inspect training dynamics and rewrite executable optimizer code during a single training run. inspect:2610.32142.question: In practical LLM fine-tuning, what accuracy, stability, and learning-rate-ratio results does the proposed initialization achieve versus tuned vanilla LoRA and standard-initialization LoRA+ at matched rank, training data, and compute?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix B B than for the down-projection matrix A A . However, the ratio η B / η A \eta_{B}/\eta_{A} itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal–noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard Init[A] , the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for B B , η B \eta_{B} , the initialization scale β \beta , and the adapter rank r r . In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] , a simple initialization that scales the variance of A A as σ A 2 ∝ n − 2 \sigma_{A}^{2}\propto n^{-2} while keeping B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 . Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of 1 / n 1/n , stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Empirically, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, Init[ A

Across tasks and models, Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard Init[A] , and makes the width-based guideline η B ≈ n ​ η A \eta_{B}\approx n\eta_{A} a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 22 ] is a standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) [ 21 , 35 , 33 ] . Given a width- n n LoRA layer with pretrained weight W ∈ ℝ n × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and input Z ¯ ∈ ℝ n \underline{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , LoRA uses Z ¯ = W ​ Z ¯ + α r ​ B ​ A ​ Z ¯ \bar{Z}=W\underline{Z}+\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\underline{Z} , where A ∈ ℝ r × n A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and B ∈ ℝ n × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} are trainable with learning rates (LRs) η A \eta_{A} and η B \eta_{B} . Here r ≪ n r\ll n is the adapter rank and α / r \alpha/r is the LoRA update multiplier. We use β \beta to denote the initialization-magnitude hyperparameter: standard LoRA initialization, denoted Init[A] , initializes B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 and initializes A 0 A_{0} randomly with mean zero and standard deviation β n − 1 / 2 \beta n^{-1/2} , so the adapter preserves the pretrained model output at step zero. Figure 1 : Overview of LoRA initialization and feature-norm stability. Left : LoRA branch notation and the initialization scalings compared in this work, including standard Init[A] , Init[AB] , and the proposed Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] . Right : feature-norm trajectories at width n = 4096 n=4096 for different initialization scales β \beta . Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] keeps the LoRA features nearly invariant to β \beta , while the alternative scalings exhibit stronger initialization-dependent growth.

Despite its simplicity, LoRA is sensitive to hyperparameters (HPs). The rank r r controls the expressive capacity of the adapter [ 60 ] , but its effect is inseparable from the update multiplier λ r = α / r \lambda_{r}=\alpha/r . Kalajdzievski [ 27 ] shows that the conventional choice α / r \alpha/r is not rank-stabilized: it can shrink adapter activations and gradients as r r grows, slowing learning at high ranks and motivating the alternative α / r \alpha/\sqrt{r} . LRs introduce a further source of brittleness. Recent empirical work shows that, after sufficiently broad LR sweeps, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants [ 32 ] . This shifts the practical question from only designing new adapters to understanding LoRA HP selection. LoRA+ [ 17 ] gives a principled route toward understanding LR selection by assigning different LRs to the two LoRA matrices. Its infinite-width feature learning analysis suggests that efficient LoRA feature updates require an asymmetric regime with η B ≫ η A \eta_{B}\gg\eta_{A} and, under idealized scaling assumptions, a ratio η B / η A ≈ n \eta_{B}/\eta_{A}\approx n . We write this ratio as ρ = η B / η A \rho=\eta_{B}/\eta_{A} . The asymmetric regime is attractive because B B directly controls the LoRA branch output, so increasing η B \eta_{B} can accelerate adaptation. In finite pretrained LLMs, however, ρ \rho often becomes another hyperparameter to tune: large ratios can improve performance, but under Init[A] they can also trigger instability. We address the gap between the theoretical LR guidance and practical LLM fine-tuning in this paper.

We show that the fragility of asymmetric LRs comes from an initialization-dependent noise term that survives even though the LoRA branch has zero output at initialization. Although B 0 = 0 B_{0}=0 , the random matrix A 0 A_{0} affects the branch as soon as B B moves away from zero. A signal–noise decomposition of the LoRA feature update reveals two components: a task-driven signal from optimizer updates and a noise term from the interaction between the learned B B and the random initial A A . Both terms scale with η B \eta_{B} , so increasing η B \eta_{B} amplifies useful adaptation and initialization noise at the same time. In the small-LR regime common in pretrained LLM fine-tuning, the signal can remain controlled while the Init[A] noise contribution does not vanish with width, making large ρ \rho , large initialization scale β \beta , and large update multiplier α / r \alpha/r especially brittle.

Previous work analyzes LoRA through a feature learning perspective, but achieving feature learning can be challenging in practice. Although Hayou et al. [17] propose the scaling η B ≫ η A \eta_{B}\gg\eta_{A} , the best ratio for a finite model still requires costly tuning. Furthermore, practical deployments may use a large LoRA update multiplier α / r \alpha/r to encourage rapid adaptation, even when LRs are small. In this section, we show that standard Init[A] then has initialization-induced noise that can accumulate over training, whereas our proposed Init[ A 2 \text{A}^{2} ] suppresses this source of instability.

inspect:2610.32878.question: For LEMS and KFAC-SVD experiments on Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3, which SVD compression baselines are compared at matched parameter budgets, calibration data, and evaluation settings, and what perplexity or zero-shot accuracy differences are reported?

passages.text: We evaluate KFAC-SVD against state-of-the-art methods across three LLM families: Mistral , Llama 3 , and Qwen3 . Table 2 details the results for all approaches under uniform compression rates (0.9, 0.7) and calibration sample count, with an additional line for our search-enhanced variant. KFAC-SVD consistently yields the lowest perplexity, with gains most pronounced on Llama 3 . At a 0.7 compression ratio, KFAC-SVD improves perplexity on WikiText2 by 49 % over the best baseline ( DOBI-SVD ), extending to 66 % with LEMS . Zero-shot accuracy largely follows this trend: under mild compression (0.9), KFAC-SVD avoids the sharp accuracy drop seen in several baselines and stays in the mid- 50 s, while LEMS recovers near-lossless performance ( 61.8 % vs. 63.3 % original). Strictly comparing to prior Fisher-based methods, KFAC-SVD outperforms the baselines by up to 10.3 p.p. without the addition of LEMS . GFWSVD degrades significantly under identical conditions, reaffirming its conditioning challenges. The only exception is Mistral at 0.9, where ASVD achieves a slightly higher zero-shot accuracy (+0.35 p.p. ) despite worse perplexity. This implies Mistral relies on features well-aligned with activation magnitude, favoring simpler proxies in uniform settings. Overall, KFAC-SVD provides the most effective decomposition, especially when compared with other Fisher-based methods, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in the vast majority of evaluated settings.

To assess the scalability of LEMS , we evaluate the Qwen3 family (4B-32B) across five compression ratios (0.5-0.9). To demonstrate that LEMS is agnostic to a particular decomposition objective, we report results for both KFAC-SVD and the activation-based SVD-LLM . Figure 2 contrasts uniform allocation (solid) to LEMS (dashed), with numerical results provided in Supplement D .

Across all budgets and model sizes, LEMS consistently improves both perplexity and downstream utility. Averaged over ratios and models, it reduces perplexity by 17% for KFAC-SVD and 34% for SVD-LLM , while increasing zero-shot accuracy by +7.2 and +9.1 p.p. , respectively. Gains are largest under aggressive compression: at 0.5, LEMS cuts perplexity by ∼ \sim 26% ( KFAC-SVD ) / ∼ \sim 57% ( SVD-LLM ) on average and recovers +4.8 / +8.7 p.p. accuracy. Crucially, it also resolves the sharp accuracy dips observed in Qwen3 -32B under uniform allocation for both decompositions. The benefits extend beyond Qwen3 : on the substantially larger Llama 3 .1-70B, LEMS reduces WikiText2 perplexity from 7.9 to 4.5 and increases accuracy from 62.6 to 66.6 (see Supplement B.6 ). Comparing decompositions methods, KFAC-SVD achieves approximately 26% lower perplexity than SVD-LLM under uniform allocation, demonstrating stronger alignment with the downstream loss. When combined with LEMS , perplexities become tightly matched between the two methods, with SVD-LLM retaining a marginal edge in zero-shot accuracy ( ∼ \sim 0.3 p.p. ). Notably, the larger gains observed for SVD-LLM with LEMS suggest that suboptimal rank allocation is often a primary source of degradation under uniform compression. Differently, through the calibrated layer-wise error model and global ILP optimization, LEMS overcomes the degradation of uniform compression yielding consistent gains.

In deployment, however, the appropriate fairness action can vary across requests because the candidate pool, item metadata, exposure debt, user preference history, and utility budget all change at runtime. We propose FAIRGate, a model-agnostic delivery controller that places an agentic policy-selection layer between a base ranker and the final top-K list. The agent does not define fairness objectives from scratch. matches.title: Cross-Pollination Retrieval: Finding Transferable Ideas Across Fields in Scientific Literature
matches.abstract_excerpt: Many scientific advances come from cross-pollination, carrying an idea from one field over to a problem in another. Yet retrieving papers across fields remains underexplored, with existing benchmarks confined to a narrow range of fields. We study cross-pollination retrieval, the problem of identifying transferable ideas across research fields, and introduce CPR-Dataset, a large-scale dataset constructed by mining cross-topic citations. Its evaluation split CPR-eval has 1,300 queries in 26 fields, and its training split CPR-train has 10,573 pairs. matches.title: Modeling Authentic Research Trajectories: A Graph View of Research Ideation
matches.abstract_excerpt: The research idea in a published paper is rarely the project's initial idea. Between the two lies a closed-loop process in which researchers run experiments, derive insights, identify challenges, explore the literature, and revise the idea, with each step motivated by evidence and reasoning they can articulate. inspect:2610.29812.question: In the SciFact harness ablation, how do ReAct query writing, single-shot retrieval, and the oracle compare on gold-paper recall, verdict accuracy, citation correctness, and cost under fixed backbones and output format? Which differences are statistically significant?

passages.text: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49–59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79–86% accuracy, a significant 17–24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers .

Language agents that search the biomedical literature are quickly becoming a default component of scientific assistants: they formulate queries, read abstracts, and return verdicts with citations ( Lála et al., 2023 ; Skarlinski et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2024 ) . The design space of such harnesses is large, but the empirical basis for choosing among designs is thin. Three questions arise for anyone building a literature agent for the life sciences: (i) Does giving a frontier model access to PubMed improve its verdicts over closed-book answering, or does parametric knowledge suffice? (ii) Is an agentic loop, in which the model writes and refines its own queries ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Nakano et al., 2021 ) , worth its additional cost over a fixed one-shot retrieval pipeline ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) ? (iii) When agents cite papers, are those citations faithful to what they actually read? We study these questions in a controlled setting: expert-written biomedical claim verification on SciFact ( Wadden et al., 2020 ) , using the live PubMed E-utilities API as the only tool. We hold the backbone model, prompt format, and output schema fixed and vary only the harness : closed-book, single-shot retrieval, a ReAct-style multi-query agent, and an oracle that receives the gold abstracts. We run the same protocol with two backbones and decompose errors into retrieval failures (the gold paper was never seen) and reasoning failures (the gold paper was seen but the verdict was wrong).

Table 1: Claim verification on 100 SciFact dev claims (95% bootstrap CIs in brackets). Gold recall: fraction of Support / Contradict claims ( n = 64 n{=}64 ) for which a SciFact gold abstract was retrieved. #Searches: mean PubMed queries per claim. Backbone Harness Acc. (%) Macro-F1 (%) Gold recall (%) #Searches Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite Closed-book 55.0 [45,64] 46.5 [38,55] – – Single-shot RAG 53.0 [44,63] 52.5 [41,62] 6 1.00 Agentic search 62.0 [52,71] 60.3 [50,69] 19 1.42 Oracle abstracts 86.0 [79,92] 85.8 [78,92] – – Gemini-3.5-Flash-Lite Closed-book 59.0 [49,69] 53.6 [44,63] – – Single-shot RAG 49.0 [39,59] 46.0 [35,57] 6 1.00 Agentic search 62.0 [52,71] 61.1 [50,70] 20 1.70 Oracle abstracts 79.0 [71,87] 78.6 [70,86] – – Figure 1: (a) Macro-F1 by harness with 95% bootstrap CIs. (b) Accuracy on Support / Contradict claims, split by whether a gold abstract was retrieved (gold-hit groups are small: n = 4 n{=}4 for RAG and n = 12 / 13 n{=}12/13 for the agent). Table 1 and Figure 1 summarize the results. We highlight five findings. F1: Naive one-shot retrieval does not help, and changes how the model fails. Issuing the claim itself as a PubMed query retrieves a gold abstract for only 6% of evidence-bearing claims (4/64 for both backbones). Given mostly off-target abstracts, both models abstain heavily: 59% and 70% of their predictions are NEI, against 36% NEI in the gold labels. Accuracy is unchanged or lower relative to closed-book (53.0 vs. 55.0 and 49.0 vs. 59.0; exact McNemar p = 0.89 p{=}0.89 and p = 0.24 p{=}0.24 ). Retrieval converts overconfident errors into abstentions rather than into correct verdicts. When the gold abstract was retrieved, both models were correct on all 4 such claims.

F2: Letting the model write its own queries triples gold recall and gives the best verdicts, but the gains are modest. The agentic harness raises gold recall to 19–20% and attains the highest accuracy (62.0 for both backbones) and macro-F1 (60.3 and 61.1) of the non-oracle harnesses. Its queries are short, entity-centric reformulations (e.g., “chenodeoxycholic acid energy expenditure” instead of the full claim), and they can repair misspellings in the claim ( “Chenodeosycholic” → \rightarrow “chenodeoxycholic” ), which silently break literal retrieval. In paired comparisons, however, the improvement is not statistically significant at N = 100 N{=}100 : agent vs. single-shot, 24 vs. 15 discordant claims ( p = 0.20 p{=}0.20 ) and 29 vs. 16 ( p = 0.07 p{=}0.07 ); agent vs. closed-book, 13 vs. 6 ( p = 0.17 p{=}0.17 ) and 11 vs. 8 ( p = 0.65 p{=}0.65 ). The direction is consistent across both backbones. F3: Agents under-use their search budget. Despite a budget of 4 searches, the agents issue 1.42 and 1.70 queries per claim on average and answer after a single search on 71% and 55% of claims; only 3% and 6% of claims use the full budget. Among evidence-bearing claims where the agent never saw a gold abstract, it still answered Support / Contradict correctly 75% of the time, suggesting that it draws on other relevant PubMed papers or on parametric knowledge. But it also abstains less on true NEI claims (33% and 42% NEI recall, versus 72% and 81% for single-shot). Budget use is therefore a clear axis for harness improvement, for example through a minimum-evidence criterion before answering.

Implications for harness design. (1) Query formulation appears to be where the model adds the most value in a literature agent: letting the LLM reformulate the query triples recall of the right paper and gives the best verdicts on both backbones, whereas passing the claim straight to the search engine does not help. (2) The largest remaining headroom lies in retrieval, as the 17–24 point gap to the oracle shows, so iterative search that is actually used (F3), citation chasing, and domain retrievers are more promising than stronger verdict prompting. (3) Citations from ungrounded generation should never be surfaced, even when the IDs resolve: validating that a PMID exists is not sufficient, and relevance must be checked against the retrieved text. Limitations. This is a pilot study. N = 100 N{=}100 claims per condition gives wide confidence intervals, and none of the accuracy differences between realistic harnesses is significant. Both backbones are small, efficient models from a single provider, chosen for their low latency and cost, so results may differ for larger or open-weight models. SciFact labels are defined with respect to specific cited abstracts, whereas our harnesses search all of PubMed as of 2026. Some “errors” may therefore reflect newer or different evidence, and title-matched gold recall is a lower bound on useful retrieval. Relevance judgments come from a single LLM judge, validated only on 50 controls. We plan to scale to the full dev set, add open-weight and biomedical-specialist backbones, and study budget-forcing strategies for agentic search.

Reproducibility. Code, prompts, all raw model outputs, and the cached PubMed responses are available at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers . The released cache reproduces every reported number without API access.

Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) has emerged as a strong optimizer for training large neural networks. The same direction is shared by a broader family of matrix optimizers. It is the steepest-descent direction for the spectral norm, used in stochastic spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2015a ; Carlson et al., 2016 ; Carlson et al., 2015b ) and revisited by Bernstein and Newhouse (2024) . It is also the linear-minimization-oracle (LMO) direction of norm-constrained methods ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) , and Shampoo ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) reduces to it when preconditioner accumulation is switched off ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) . Controlled benchmarks place such matrix-based optimizers among the strongest available ( Wen et al., 2026 ) , so understanding when a step along polar ⁡ ( G ) \mathrm{polar}(G) helps matters well beyond Muon .

Existing analyses view these methods as non-Euclidean trust-region ( Kovalev, 2025 ) or LMO-based steepest descent ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) and provide convergence guarantees for Muon ( Li and Hong, 2025 ) . These are worst-case bounds over broad function classes, governed by smoothness constants in the chosen norm and by norm-equivalence factors; where they suggest an advantage over (stochastic) gradient descent ( GD ), it comes from comparing such constants across norms ( Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Davis and Drusvyatskiy, 2025 ) . They do not separate the effect of the orthogonalized direction from that of the step-size scale set by these constants, so when this direction improves on the gradient step remains open. Analyses of Muon with finite Newton--Schulz treat it as an approximation of the polar factor whose error worsens the guarantees ( Shulgin et al., 2026 ; Kim and Oh, 2026 ; Takezawa et al., 2026 ) , related work attributes this error to ill-conditioning and replaces the solver ( Refael et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) , and improved solvers aim to reduce it ( Cesista et al., 2025 ; Grishina et al., 2025 ; Amsel et al., 2026 ) .

Gonon et al. (2026) also study Muon on quadratics. On the isotropic quadratic, exact polar steps with a constant step size can fail to reach the minimizer, and random perturbations of the polar step restore reachability in a one-dimensional model; on general Hessians, they show numerically that the comparison with GD depends on the shape of the spectrum, that Newton--Schulz can help or hurt, and that a direction that wins at every step need not win along the trajectory. Our one-step and trajectory results are exact for any positive-definite Hessian. We relate our one-step condition to Davis and Drusvyatskiy (2025) in Section 2 and discuss other work in the sections where it is relevant.

We isolated the geometry of the orthogonalized update shared by Muon and related matrix optimizers by analyzing PolarGD on matrix quadratics. PolarGD benefits from orthogonal equivariance and implicit preconditioning by the iterate, but it is not uniformly better than GD or SignGD : it is fast near row-isotropic iterates and slow near rank deficiency, where exact polar normalization overweights tiny singular values. Finite Newton--Schulz softens the update exactly there and can then converge faster than exact polar, so it is not merely an approximation of the polar factor. The trajectory results rely on the quadratic structure, but Proposition 1 only needs the curvature bounds ( 2 ), and equivariance and the softening by Newton--Schulz hold for any objective, including the momentum matrix that Muon orthogonalizes. Our transformer measurements show that the regime where exact polar and Newton--Schulz differ occurs in practice. This suggests treating the number of Newton--Schulz steps, or the damping level, as a design choice of the optimizer rather than only as an accuracy setting.

inspect:2610.28072.question: On the 64 LoRA fine-tuning problems, how does MuPACE compare with per-task tuned fixed schedules at matched training budget, including Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B transfer? What meta-training and inference overhead is reported?

passages.text: Learning rate schedules are typically fixed before training begins, yet when fine-tuning large language models with low-rank adapters (LoRA), the appropriate scale varies substantially with the model, task, and adapter configuration. Practitioners re-tune a schedule for every new problem, yet a tuned schedule still cannot react to the training dynamics it encounters. We instead amortize learning rate selection across LoRA fine-tuning problems. We leave the base optimizer, Muon, untouched, so that its normalized update fixes the direction, and meta-learn only the global step size. Our method MuPACE is a small recurrent policy, meta-trained across a distribution of fine-tuning runs, that conditions on the observed trajectory and emits bounded adjustments to an interpretable analytic schedule. On 64 fine-tuning problems, MuPACE outperforms standard fixed schedules at a strong shared default on 64–78% of problems and is on par with the same schedules with per-task tuned peaks. Meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, MuPACE transfers one-shot to unseen tasks on models as deep as 64 layers, such as Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, where a single run remains competitive with swept schedules.

We therefore ask the following question: Can learning rate schedule selection instead be amortized across LoRA fine-tuning problems? We introduce MuPACE ( Mu on P olicy for A daptive C ontrol across LoRA Fine-tuning E pisodes), a learned, trajectory-conditioned learning rate scheduler for LoRA. LoRA fine-tuning is especially relevant because only a few large organizations train large language models from scratch, while most users adapt existing pretrained models ( Bommasani et al., 2021 ) . Unlike previous learned optimizers that meta-learn the update rule itself ( Metz et al., 2022b ; Moudgil et al., 2025 ) , we leave Muon unchanged and meta-learn only its global step-size schedule. A small recurrent policy observes the optimization trajectory and predicts bounded modifications to an analytic schedule family, explicitly separating changes in overall scale from changes in schedule shape. The scheduler is meta-trained across a distribution of fine-tuning episodes and then applied one-shot to new problems, producing an adaptive schedule within a single training run without hyperparameter search or downstream-specific tuning.

To assess the effectiveness of our approach, we evaluate whether a single meta-trained scheduler can replace per-task learning rate search across a broad range of fine-tuning settings, spanning pretrained models, downstream tasks, adapter configurations, batch sizes, and training horizons. On 64 problems, MuPACE outperforms strong fixed defaults on 64–78% of tasks and performs on par with schedules tuned separately for each problem, while requiring only a single trial. Moreover, despite being meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, MuPACE generalizes in a one-shot manner to large-scale models such as Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B (both with 64 layers) on unseen downstream tasks. It achieves competitive performance close to that of swept schedules while requiring only a single run. Our key contributions are: • We introduce MuPACE , a meta-learned, trajectory-conditioned learning rate scheduler for LoRA fine-tuning that adapts a bounded analytic schedule while leaving the base optimizer, Muon, unchanged, enabling one-shot application without target-task learning rate search. • We show that a single meta-trained scheduler generalizes across fine-tuning problems and model scales. On 64 problems, MuPACE outperforms strong fixed defaults and performs comparably to per-task tuned schedules, while transferring one-shot to Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B on unseen tasks, where it remains competitive with tuned learning rate schedules in a single run.

We transfer MuPACE one-shot to Qwen3-32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Qwen3.8-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) . Both have 64 64 layers and width 5120 5120 , against at most 16 16 layers and width 2048 2048 in the meta-training deck. Further, Qwen3.8-27B adds a hybrid Gated DeltaNet linear-attention architecture the policy never saw. Adapters use r = 8 r=8 , a = 16 a=16 and T = 200 T=200 steps on eight unseen datasets spanning instruction following, math, code, summarization, question answering and translation ( Section A.1 ). We report test loss at the iteration with the lowest validation loss. For fixed-schedule baselines, we additionally select the peak learning rate from five log-spaced values in [ 10 − 5 , 10 − 3 ] [10^{-5},10^{-3}] , while MuPACE and each Hypergradient Descent variant use a single run.

The tuned baselines reach slightly lower test loss, with median relative differences of 1.13 % 1.13\% – 2.43 % 2.43\% on Qwen3-32B and 2.59 % 2.59\% – 3.02 % 3.02\% on Qwen3.8-27B, and MuPACE wins on 2 2 of 8 8 datasets per model. This gap is the price of one run versus five. Given only one trial, the fixed schedules perform worse than MuPACE by 14 % 14\% – 18 % 18\% on average and need two to three trials to reach the same performance (Appendix C ). Against Hypergradient Descent, the other sweep-free method, MuPACE achieves lower test loss on every dataset for both models, whether Hypergradient Descent is used with or without μ \mu P post-scaling. We ask whether MuPACE still outperforms the fixed schedules when the latter are given the same depth-dependent scaling and their learning-rate peaks are selected without any target-task search. Specifically, we apply the learned policy’s depth- μ \mu P multiplier from Equation 6 to cosine, WSD, and constant schedules on both out-of-distribution models. For each schedule family, we transfer (i) the default peak of 10 − 3 10^{-3} and (ii) the best fixed peak from a sweep on the in-distribution evaluation, denoted p ∗ p^{*} . For WSD and constant, the source-selected and default peaks coincide. Thus, the comparison tests whether MuPACE provides gains beyond transferring either default or source-tuned depth-scaled fixed schedules. All arms report test loss at their own best-validation checkpoint. Target-tuned schedules and Hypergradient Descent are shown for context. Depth-scaled fixed schedules use no target-task peak selection.

passages.text: Binary-weight language models store one bit per weight, but training them keeps a full-precision latent copy of each weight plus Adam state, about 96 extra bits per weight, so a deployed binary model cannot be adapted on the device that runs it. We replace the latent weight with a 2–8-bit residual buffer quantized by stochastic rounding, which cuts the training state per weight from 97 bits to 3–9, up to 19 × 19\times less. The resulting error-diffusion (ED) optimizer moves the residual-carrying loop of image halftoning onto the weight-update path. Each buffer accumulates the unrealized part of every update and flips the weight when the accumulated value crosses a threshold, and it works only when its quantization grid has a level exactly at that threshold. Under this threshold-alignment rule, 4-bit buffers match 8-bit buffers on a binary multilayer perceptron benchmark, and the same rule lifts a different latent-free optimizer, Bop, from a 10-point deficit at 4 bits to full-precision accuracy. On character-level transformers with 97% of parameters binary, ED trains within 5–11% of the latent-weight reference at a 2,000-step budget and within 1.7% at convergence. On scaling ladders over enwik8 and wikitext-103, up to 19M parameters on enwik8 (70M with the wikitext-103 embeddings), the latent-free loss stays within − 2.3 % -2.3\% to + 2.9 % +2.9\% of the reference at all six sizes once a per-step cap on the buffer update removes a launch instability (§ 5.4 ); without the cap it trails by 10% at the largest tokenized size. ED at one tenth of the latent training state, matching latent-weight continuation, and a fused CPU kernel completes the adaptation within a 275 MB training-memory budget, which latent-weight training cannot. A 250-step probe sets the flip learning rate at any new scale.

1. We propose ED, whose entire per-weight training state is one sign bit plus a 2–8-bit SR-quantized error-feedback buffer, 19 × 19\times less than latent-weight training at 4 bits (§ 3 ). 2. We show that the buffer is a stochastic accumulate-and-fire unit whose grid must contain a level at the flip threshold, a rule that removes an apparent 4-bit floor and restores full-precision accuracy to dithered Bop at 4 bits (§ 5.1 ). 3. We show that 97%-binary transformers train within 5–11% of the latent reference at 2,000 steps and 1.7% at convergence, that the loss tracks the reference at all six ladder sizes once a per-step update cap removes a launch instability, and that a deployed model continues training on a CPU within a 275 MB training-memory budget (§ 5.2 –§ 5.5 ). 4. We give a 250-step probe that sets the flip learning rate at a new scale, validated by a pre-registered prediction (§ 5.6 ).

Every reported cell carries bits of persistent training state per weight (b/wt). FP32+Adam carries 96, BitNet-style latent training 97, Bop 33, bf16 mixed precision 112, and ED 1 + b 1{+}b for b ∈ { 2 , … , 8 } b\in\{2,\dots,8\} (3 b/wt–9 b/wt). The clamp adds an off-grid rail state ( 2 b + 1 2^{b}{+}1 reachable values, 4.09 bits at b = 4 b{=}4 ), which we round down to b b bits in favor of ED. Per-layer weight scales, per-batch activation scales, and the FP embeddings, LayerNorms, and head of the transformers are excluded from the per-weight count (§ 4 ).

The tasks are a synthetic MLP benchmark and language models with at most 19M parameters (70M with the wikitext-103 embeddings) and six layers on one GPU, evaluated by validation loss and synthetic accuracy, not downstream tasks. The 50,000-step and tokenized-ladder cells are single runs, so the small margins among the converged methods are not statistically separated. We do not claim wall-clock efficiency, the cost of generating SR bits is not measured, and every ladder size trains on fixed data, so the data dimension is untested ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) . The FP remnant (embeddings, norms, head, and their Adam state) is now the dominant residual training memory. The 1-bit-gradient ablation (Appendix E ) is scoped to the weight-gradient operand and shows that gradient bits and buffer bits should not both be cut aggressively. We claim no accuracy advantage over a well-built saturating integer latent weight (§ 5.1 ).

ED trains binary-weight MLPs and transformers on 3–9 bits of training state per weight, up to 19 × 19\times less than latent-weight training, by carrying each weight’s unrealized update in a stochastically rounded buffer whose grid has a level at the flip threshold. With a per-step cap on the buffer update, the loss stays within − 2.3 % -2.3\% to + 2.9 % +2.9\% of the latent reference at all six ladder sizes (§ 5.4 ), and a deployed binary model continues training on a CPU within a 275 MB training-memory budget. The FP remnant is the next target.

inspect:2610.33846.question: What CIFAR-10 architectures, random-label fractions, training controls, and test-error trajectories support the claim that deeper convolutional networks do not benefit from early stopping after memorizing noisy labels? How does the kernel-gradient-flow phase diagram relate to those neural-network experiments?

passages.text: Early stopping is commonly used to prevent fitting label noise from degrading generalization. Does this mean that, when a positive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable, the best test error must occur before interpolation? Experiments on a CIFAR10 classification task with randomly labeled examples motivate the opposite possibility: although fixed-feature and shallow models exhibit late-time deterioration of the test error, the need for early stopping essentially disappears in larger, deeper convolutional networks even after the random labels have all been classified correctly. We determine when late-time deterioration disappears entirely in a solvable setting. For kernel gradient flow on a synthetic noisy classification task, we derive sharp high-dimensional learning curves and obtain a phase diagram controlled by the balance between the linear kernel component that learns the shared relation between inputs and labels and the higher-order components that enable fitting the label noise. In one regime, generalization is optimized at finite time and early stopping is necessary. In another, generalization improves until interpolation, but the endpoint is suboptimal across kernels. At the boundary, the interpolating endpoint attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, even with extensive irreducible label noise, interpolation can outperform early stopping. The neural-network experiments leave open how learned representations acquire an analogous favorable geometry.

Figure 1: Generalization along the path to memorization. Test error on 2000 cats and dogs ( x x -axes) versus classification error on the randomly labelled automobiles ( y y -axes) taken from the CIFAR10 dataset. The fixed training set has n = 7000 n=7000 images: 2800 2800 cats, 2800 2800 dogs with their respective labels, and 1400 1400 automobiles with independent random labels. Panels vary the overparametrization ratio κ = P / n ≈ 1 , 10 , 100 \kappa=P/n\approx 1,10,100 , where P P counts optimized parameters. Curves average about 30 completed seeds; a centered arithmetic average of up to seven neighboring recorded times is applied to both coordinates for display, preserving the initial and final values. These parametric curves trace the two errors as training time t t increases. Triangles mark initialization, squares the last iterate and crosses the minimum displayed test error. All trainable networks use square loss and constant-rate Nesterov SGD, without augmentation or weight decay, through 1500 epochs; RF-CNN uses full-batch readout GD through 10 12 10^{12} steps. In Appendix F we provide all numerical details and the unsmoothed trajectories, including training loss.

We challenge this expectation through a controlled experiment based on CIFAR10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) . Cats and dogs define a shared classification task, while automobile images, comprising 20% of the training set, receive fixed random labels. We measure the generalization error on new samples of cats and dogs and the memorization error, defined as the fraction of misclassified automobiles in the training set, to track when the unpredictable labels have been fitted. Figure 1 follows the two errors jointly as training progresses across architectures and model sizes. Fixed-feature and smaller or shallower models exhibit the familiar behavior: as the memorization error decreases, the test performance eventually deteriorates. For the larger, deeper convolutional and residual networks, this deterioration is essentially absent: their best observed test performance is attained with zero memorization error, and early stopping does not visibly improve generalization. Empirical hypothesis. In image classification, even with extensive label noise, large, deep neural networks with competitive test performance do not benefit from early stopping.

We derive exact learning curves and obtain a phase diagram with three regimes, corresponding to three families of kernels. In the first, test error reaches its minimum at finite time and subsequently increases, so early stopping is necessary. In the second, test error improves until convergence, but the resulting interpolating predictor is suboptimal relative to other kernel geometries. Precisely at the boundary between these regimes, gradient flow converges to an interpolating predictor that attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel families and all training times. Thus, even in the presence of extensive label noise, interpolation can lead to a better test error than any early stopping. The kernel analysis therefore produces the behavior that motivated this work. At the critical geometry, the best test error is attained at interpolation, and the corresponding trajectory in Figure 4 closely resembles those of the larger, deeper neural networks in Figure 1 , whose best test performance is attained after all randomly labelled examples have been classified correctly. The theory thus provides a concrete realization of the observed phenomenon. It does not, however, explain how neural-network training constructs a representation with analogous properties. Determining which aspects of feature learning, model size, and architecture produce this behavior remains an open question.

In this work, we asked whether the presence of extensive label noise necessarily makes early stopping preferable to interpolation. The noisy CIFAR10 experiments in Fig. 1 and Appendix F support the hypothesis that deep and highly overparameterized neural networks actually do not benefit from early stopping. Figure 1 shows that the larger and deeper networks attain their best observed test performance only after their memorization error reaches zero, while fixed-feature and shallower models exhibit late-time test-error deterioration. Appendix F shows that this observation is robust beyond the setting of Fig. 1 : it persists across a range of training recipes, including cross-entropy, data augmentation, and a scheduled learning rate, as well as across additional optimization controls. We then asked whether the absence of a benefit from early stopping can be reproduced in an analytically solvable setting. Our analysis of high-dimensional learning curves for kernel gradient flow shows that it can. Kernel geometry determines whether the lowest test error occurs at a finite time or at convergence. We identify a critical kernel geometry for which the interpolating predictor attains the lowest test error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, fitting unpredictable labels need not come at the expense of generalization, in a sense yet considerably stronger than the one known from the literature on benign overfitting.

The critical-kernel trajectory provides a concrete fixed-representation counterpart of the behavior observed in the deeper neural networks: fitting the unpredictable labels does not produce a late-time deterioration of generalization, and the best test error is attained at the end of the trajectory. Our analysis does not, however, establish that the networks learn this same geometry, nor does it explain how feature learning, architecture, and optimization produce the empirically observed behavior. The theory nevertheless places the empirical hypothesis formulated in the introduction on a precise footing: even under extensive label noise, the absence of a benefit from early stopping is possible and can be controlled by representation geometry. Understanding how larger and deeper feature-learning architectures realize analogous behavior remains an open question. All the results can be reproduced using the code provided in the repository: https://github.com/SPOC-group/Early-stopping .

We challenge this expectation through a controlled experiment based on CIFAR10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) . Cats and dogs define a shared classification task, while automobile images, comprising 20% of the training set, receive fixed random labels. In the first, test error reaches its minimum at finite time and subsequently increases, so early stopping is necessary. In the second, test error improves until convergence, but the resulting interpolating predictor is suboptimal relative to other kernel geometries. Precisely at the boundary between these regimes, gradient flow converges to an interpolating predictor that attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel families and all training times. In this work, we asked whether the presence of extensive label noise necessarily makes early stopping preferable to interpolation. The noisy CIFAR10 experiments in Fig. 1 and Appendix F support the hypothesis that deep and highly overparameterized neural networks actually do not benefit from early stopping. Figure 1 shows that the larger and deeper networks attain their best observed test performance only after their memorization error reaches zero, while fixed-feature and shallower models exhibit late-time test-error deterioration. We then asked whether the absence of a benefit from early stopping can be reproduced in an analytically solvable setting. Our analysis of high-dimensional learning curves for kernel gradient flow shows that it can. Kernel geometry determines whether the lowest test error occurs at a finite time or at convergence. We identify a critical kernel geometry for which the interpolating predictor attains the lowest test error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, fitting unpredictable labels need not come at the expense of generalization, in a sense yet considerably stronger than the one known from the literature on benign overfitting.

The critical-kernel trajectory provides a concrete fixed-representation counterpart of the behavior observed in the deeper neural networks: fitting the unpredictable labels does not produce a late-time deterioration of generalization, and the best test error is attained at the end of the trajectory. Our analysis does not, however, establish that the networks learn this same geometry, nor does it explain how feature learning, architecture, and optimization produce the empirically observed behavior. The theory nevertheless places the empirical hypothesis formulated in the introduction on a precise footing: even under extensive label noise, the absence of a benefit from early stopping is possible and can be controlled by representation geometry. Understanding how larger and deeper feature-learning architectures realize analogous behavior remains an open question. All the results can be reproduced using the code provided in the repository: https://github.com/SPOC-group/Early-stopping .
